Expectation1: Listen actively and provide emotional support when needed.
Situation1: A friend sends a text message complaining about having a long, boring day.
Expectation2: Provide spiritual guidance and counseling to individuals in need
Situation2: A member of the community has scheduled an appointment to discuss a persistent personal struggle.
Story: My phone buzzed with a message from Mark: “Rough day. Can you talk?” I knew he needed me to listen, to be the friend who always made time, who never judged. I started typing a reply, but then the church bell chimed, reminding me of my next appointment. Mrs. Evans was waiting in my office, hoping for spiritual guidance about her ongoing battle with anxiety. As a priest, I was expected to be present, to offer wisdom and comfort, to help her find peace in her faith. But Mark’s words tugged at me—he counted on me to be there, to care about the little things that made up his world. I felt the weight of both roles pressing in, each demanding my full attention, each expecting me to be wholly theirs. My heart raced as I stood in the hallway, torn between the friend who needed to vent and the parishioner who needed hope. I stared at my phone, then at the office door, feeling the impossible pull of two worlds that refused to let go.
